claims.text: Rules extracted from databases by data mining techniques can be discriminatory when used for decision tasks.
Removing discriminatory attributes from a dataset is insufficient to guarantee non-discrimination when background knowledge is available.
Discriminatory rules can be formally related to apparently safe rules using background knowledge to characterize redlining.

evidence.description: Rules extracted from databases by data mining techniques, such as classification or association rules, when used for decision tasks such as benefit or credit approval, can be discriminatory.
A naive approach, like taking away all discriminatory attributes, is shown to be not enough when other background knowledge is available.
Our approach leads to a precise formulation of the redlining problem along with a formal result relating discriminatory rules with apparently safe ones by means of background knowledge.

methodologies.name: Discrimination-aware data mining
methodologies.description: A framework for defining, formalizing, and identifying discriminatory classification rules and redlining through background knowledge.

limitations.text: Naive approaches that simply remove discriminatory attributes fail to guarantee non-discrimination when background knowledge is available.
